newsitem.title: UK: UK Union chief warns Blair over reforms.
newsitem.headline: UK Union chief warns Blair over reforms.

text.p: A senior trade union leader on Thursday warned Prime Minister Tony Blair he will face stiff opposition if he tries to push through reforms curbing the influence of unions over his Labour Party.
"I don't see the trade unions voting to reduce their influence within the party," said Ken Jackson, general secretary of the Amalgamated Engineering and Electrical Union.

Blair is asking October's annual party conference to agree on a new piece of Labour policy-making machinery -- a high-level committee which he himself would head and which would draw on ideas from local policy forums.
This would downgrade the role of the conference, where trade unions hold 50 percent of the votes. Critics of the idea say it would become little more than a political rally.

The Independent newspaper named Jackson as one of six union leaders who met at a London hotel on Tuesday and agreed to "draw a line in the sand" against any further encroachment on their power within the Labour Party.
In an interview with BBC radio, Jackson did not directly confirm that the meeting had taken place.
But he said: "I don't pretend to speak for the trade unions as a whole, but I think a lot of my colleagues feel exactly the same way."
"I will not support diminishing the role of the trade unions and we would have to vote for that change."

Labour is traditionally the political wing of Britain's trade union movement, but previous reforms under Blair have tilted the balance of power within the party towards ordinary members and away from union leaders.

He is pressing on with the new plan despite strong opposition within constituency Labour Parties. A total of 89 motions opposed to the reforms have been submitted to the annual conference in Brighton, southern England. Only nine are broadly in favour.

The row over the reform plan could take the edge off celebrations at the conference of May's election victory, when the party returned to power after 18 years in opposition, winning a record-breaking 179-seat majority in parliament.
